questions.prompt: An evaluation of a permits assistant reports 81% on 400 questions, 95% interval 77% to 85%. Which statement about the interval is correct?
options: It is the range of pass rates on these 400 questions if the evaluation were rerun with the same answers
It is a plausible range for the pass rate on new questions written the same way
It is the range of pass rates the assistant will reach next year
It is the range within which 95% of individual answers fall
questions.explanation: The interval estimates the pass rate on the population the questions were sampled from.
misconceptions: Treats the fixed sample as uncertain: on these questions with these answers the rate is known
Extends the interval to a different population and time
Confuses an interval for a rate with a range of single outcomes

questions.prompt: A configuration passes 270 of 300 independent questions. What is the formula standard error of its pass rate, to two significant figures?
misconceptions: Forgets the square root: 0.09 / 300 = 0.0003, then divides again
Reports p(1 − p) without dividing by n or taking the root
Uses the number of failures as the standard error

questions.prompt: A clustered standard error is 0.030 and the naive one is 0.020 on 900 questions. How many independent questions are the 900 worth?
misconceptions: Uses the ratio of standard errors, 1.5, instead of its square
Multiplies by the ratio instead of dividing
Multiplies by the design effect instead of dividing

questions.prompt: An evaluation set has 50 documents with 10 questions each and a design effect of 3. Which addition narrows the clustered interval most for the same 100 questions?
options: Two more questions from each existing document
100 more questions from 10 new documents
Five samples per question instead of one
Dropping the 10 documents with the most failures
questions.explanation: The clustered standard error falls with the number of independent clusters; new documents add them.
misconceptions: Treats extra questions from the same document as independent evidence
Confuses within-question sampling noise with between-document clustering
Removes data selectively, which biases the score

questions.prompt: At temperature 0.8 a configuration's within-item variance is 0.12 and its between-item variance 0.09. Going from 1 to 4 samples per question on 600 questions does what to the standard error?
options: Halves it, because four times the samples is like four times the questions
Leaves it unchanged, because samples of one question are not independent
Reduces it from about 0.0187 to about 0.0141
Reduces it to zero, because sampling noise disappears
misconceptions: Treats samples as if they were new questions
Thinks repeated samples add no information at all
Forgets the between-item part, which more samples do not reduce

questions.prompt: A permits assistant gives each applicant one answer. Which estimand should the release report use as its primary score?
options: pass@5: right in at least one of five samples
pass^5: right in all five samples
The best of five samples chosen by the grader
The mean pass rate per sample
questions.explanation: An applicant sees one answer, so the expected pass rate of a single sample is the quantity that matters.
misconceptions: Describes a user who can retry and pick the right answer
Describes a stricter, consistency requirement rather than the single answer
Lets the grader choose after the fact, which no applicant can do

questions.prompt: Two configurations are compared on four metrics, each tested at 5%. The report headlines whichever metric is significant. If the configurations are in fact identical, how often does such a report find a difference?
options: About 5% of the time
More than 5%, up to about 19% if the metrics were independent
Never, because each test controls its own error
Exactly 20% of the time, four times 5%
questions.explanation: Choosing the best of several tests after the results raises the chance of at least one false win; correlated metrics give a little less than 1 − 0.95⁴.
misconceptions: Assumes the per-test error rate survives selection
Confuses per-test control with control of the whole study
Adds the rates instead of combining them, and ignores correlation

questions.prompt: Which plan field, left empty, most directly allows the analyst to change the conclusion after seeing the results?
options: The decision rule linking each possible interval to an action
The owner's name
The list of secondary metrics
The date the evaluation ran
questions.explanation: Without a decision rule written in advance, any interval can be read as supporting the preferred action.
misconceptions: Names who is accountable but does not fix any analysis choice
Secondary results are labelled exploratory anyway
The run date is recorded by the logs and does not drive a conclusion
